passage_text: Researchers investigated the impact of caffeine on short‑term memory recall in healthy adults. One hundred and twenty participants were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a placebo group, a low‑dose caffeine group (50 mg), a medium‑dose caffeine group (150 mg), and a high‑dose caffeine group (300 mg). After a 30‑minute absorption period, all participants completed a standardized word‑list recall test. The researchers measured the percentage of words correctly recalled for each group. The study aimed to determine whether increasing caffeine dosage improves recall performance and whether there is a dose‑response relationship. The findings were summarized in Table 1 below, which lists the mean recall percentages and standard deviations for each dosage condition. The authors concluded that moderate caffeine intake enhances memory recall relative to placebo, but excessive intake does not yield additional benefits.
stem: Based on Table 1, which caffeine dosage group achieved the highest mean recall percentage?
explanation: The medium‑dose group (150 mg) reported a mean recall of 82.3 %, which is higher than the other groups.
trap: Students often assume that the highest dose yields the best performance, overlooking the slight decline at 300 mg.

stem: What is the main purpose of randomly assigning the 120 participants to the four dosage groups?

options.A: To make it likely that pre-existing differences in memory ability are spread evenly across the groups
options.B: To ensure every participant has exactly the same baseline recall ability
options.C: To make sure participants know which dose they received
options.D: To increase the recall percentage of the caffeine groups

explanation: Correct: Random assignment spreads pre-existing differences (such as memory ability) across groups by chance, reducing systematic bias. Why the others are wrong: B) randomization balances groups on average; it does not make individuals identical. C) randomization has no role in telling participants their dose. D) assignment method does not change recall in any group.
trap: Assuming randomization guarantees identical groups, when it only balances them on average by chance.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by Table 1?

options.A: Mean recall rose from placebo through the 150 mg dose.
options.B: The 300 mg group recalled a higher percentage than the 50 mg group.
options.C: The 300 mg group had the highest mean recall of all four groups.
options.D: The 150 mg group had the smallest SD.

explanation: Correct: The 300 mg mean (80.7%) is below the 150 mg mean (82.3%), so the high-dose group did not have the highest recall. Why the others are wrong: A) 68.4, 75.1 and 82.3% rise at each step. B) 80.7% is greater than 75.1%. D) SD of 4.5 is smaller than 5.2, 4.8 and 5.0.
trap: Assuming the highest dose must give the best recall, overlooking the small decline from 82.3% to 80.7%.

stem: Which interpretation of the 150 mg versus 300 mg results in Table 1 is best supported?

options.A: The 300 mg group recalled 1.6 percentage points less than the 150 mg group, so doubling the dose gave no added recall benefit.
options.B: The 300 mg group recalled less than the placebo group, so the high dose impaired memory.
options.C: The 300 mg group recalled exactly the same percentage as the 150 mg group.
options.D: The decline at 300 mg proves caffeine at that dose is toxic.

explanation: Correct: A) 82.3 - 80.7 = 1.6 points lower at 300 mg, while both caffeine groups remain above placebo (68.4), so no additional benefit appeared. Why the others are wrong: B) 80.7% is well above the placebo 68.4%. C) The means are 82.3% and 80.7%, not equal. D) Toxicity was not measured in the study.
trap: Reading the small decline from 82.3% to 80.7% as harm; the 300 mg group still recalled about 12 points more than placebo, so the data show no added benefit rather than impairment.
